title: Substitutable subtypes
idea: The Liskov Substitution Principle (LSP) says a subtype must work anywhere its parent type is expected, keeping every promise the parent's contract makes.

analogy.text: You book "a compact rental car". Any compact the desk hands over must start, steer and take normal fuel. One needing special fuel breaks your booking.
analogy.breaks: A clerk warns you of a swap; Java swaps silently at runtime.

points: Preconditions (what callers must supply) may not get stricter in a subtype.
Postconditions (what the method guarantees) may not get weaker; no surprise exceptions either.
Compiling proves nothing about promises; run the parent's tests against every subtype.
If a subtype cannot keep a promise, change the contract or drop inheritance.

hero.title: A subtype that breaks a promise

messages.label: add("email")
messages.note: The client was written against the parent contract: `add` keeps every job.

messages.label: add("invoice")
messages.note: Second job fits. The bounded queue is now full.

messages.label: add("backup")
messages.note: The override returns normally but drops the job. No exception, no log line.

messages.label: drain()
messages.note: The client asks for the jobs it believes are queued.

messages.label: [email, invoice]
messages.note: Three submitted, two returned. The parent's postcondition was weakened: a silent LSP break.

messages.label: offer("backup")
messages.note: Replay with the fix: a fresh BoundedJobQueue(2) already holds email and invoice. `offer` may reject, and says so in its return value.

messages.label: false
messages.note: The queue is full, so it returns false. Rejection is now part of the promise every `JobQueue` keeps.

messages.label: add("backup")
messages.note: The client handles false and keeps the job. Any subtype now substitutes safely.

code.title: The problem
code.caption: A bounded subclass overrides `add` and quietly drops a job the parent promised to keep.

walk.text: The parent's contract: `add` keeps every job. Callers were written and tested against that.
The subclass compiles and passes its own tests, so the type system raises no alarm.
When full, the override returns normally and discards the job. The postcondition is weaker.
`runAll` trusts the contract and reports three submissions. It cannot notice the drop.
Same client, two queues. Only the subtype's run loses a job, and nothing is thrown.

code.title: The fix
code.caption: Rejection becomes part of the contract, so every queue can keep the same promise.

walk.text: The contract now admits rejection: `offer` returns false, like `java.util.Queue` does.
`ListJobQueue` holds the list. `final` methods stop subclasses bending `offer` or `drain`.
`UnboundedJobQueue` always has room, so its `offer` always returns true.
`BoundedJobQueue` validates its capacity and answers only one question: is there room?
`submitAll` checks every result and keeps rejected jobs for retry. It works for any `JobQueue`.
Both queues go through the same client, and no job disappears without the client knowing.

pitfalls: An override that throws "not supported" breaks callers; give that type a smaller interface instead.
An override that silently ignores input, like a full queue dropping jobs, hides data loss.
Inheriting only to reuse code creates is-a lies; prefer composition when the promises differ.

quiz.q: `ReadOnlyStore extends Store`, and its `put` throws. The parent's `put` promises to save. What fixes the LSP break?
options: Catch the exception in every caller
ReadOnlyStore implements a read-only interface Store extends
Make put return silently instead of throwing
quiz.why: A read-only type cannot keep a promise to save. Give it a smaller contract with only reads; `Store` adds `put`, so no subtype lies.

takeaway: A subtype must keep every promise its parent made.
